rv.q: Sadly we will never know, but I cannot imagine anyone who loves theatre not being bowled over by this life-enhancing, brilliantly uninhibited, all-singing and dancing (and let’s not forget the incontinent talking) adaptation.
When Emma Rice does it, it feels madly English and, for all the other-worldliness, rooted.

It's certainly flawed, overlong and occasionally whimsical. But it's also gently touching and subtly melancholic: in the end it is about family, belonging, transience and forgiveness. An emphatic, joyous return.
‘Wise Children’ (the play) is a gleefully breakneck night of storytelling that relishes in the many lurid details of the extremely complex story of intertwined Chance and Hazard clans.
This makes for a messy and often melancholy experience, frequently magical and pleasingly weird; not Rice’s most soaring work perhaps but still a joy.
Emma Rice does justice to the verve and racy humour of Carter's writing, and the result is a pleasing oddity, tinged with melancholy yet joyous and inventive.
On the stage (which you would imagine is the novel's natural milieu), the lack of pulse-quickening drama is hard to conceal.
For all her signature whimsical charm (bobble-hats, check; butterflies, check), that's what makes 'Wise Children' Rice's most sophisticated show yet.
It’s a love letter to theatre for people who love theatre.

So it's somewhat disheartening to report that the play bearing her new creative endeavour's name is a decidedly mixed bag: exposition-heavy and tonally scattershot, while also freewheeling and fun and occasionally touching (especially after the interval).

Emma Rice and the late Angela Carter make a fine match – their works are full of invention, wit and fantasy. This new adaptation of Carter’s 1991 novel is a great yarn that distils, through its fairy-tale exaggerations, themes of family that are universal while being original and surprising.
Her inaugural show at the Old Vic is a joyful love letter to all things theatre, a tangle of surreal comedy and convoluted family drama.
The production, which Rice describes as a love letter to theatre, matches the exuberance of the original novel and revels in its whimsicality, diversity, theatricality.

cn.t: Emma Rice's exuberant adaptation of Angela Carter's novel marks a joyful return to form, bursting with theatrical invention and infectious energy, though some critics find it occasionally excessive in its creative abundance.
